s0.why: [1] says emerald is a gemstone and beryl variety coloured green by trace chromium or sometimes vanadium.

s1.why: [20] says emeralds tend to have numerous inclusions and fissures; [23] says almost all are oiled to enhance apparent clarity.

s2.why: [8] makes colour the most important criterion; [18] and [26] give well saturated, vivid green and medium-dark tone for the best stones.

f0.why: [2] gives beryl, the mineral emerald is a variety of, a hardness of 7.5 to 8 on the Mohs scale.

f1.why: [24] says inclusions and fissures are called jardin, French for garden, for their mossy appearance.

f2.why: [29] says most emeralds are oiled to fill surface-reaching cracks; [30] says cedar oil is often used.

f3.why: [44] says emeralds were mined in Ancient Egypt on Mount Smaragdus since 1500 BC.

f4.why: [28] calls the emerald cut the signature cut, rectangular with facets around the top edge.

q1.why: [16] says only medium to dark gems are emeralds and light-toned ones are called green beryl.

q2.why: [2] gives the 7.5 to 8 hardness; [3] says many inclusions make toughness poor.

q3.why: [35] says oil-treated emeralds are worth much less than untreated ones of similar quality.

q4.why: [21] contrasts the diamond 10x loupe standard with emeralds graded by eye; [22] defines flawless as no eye-visible inclusions.

q5.why: [37] says green-tinted oil is not acceptable in the trade; [35] says ordinary oiling is largely accepted.

q6.why: [27] says relative non-uniformity motivates cabochon cutting rather than faceted shapes.
